title: Introduction to Agentic Coding
description: Learn how AI coding agents go beyond suggestions — planning, executing multi-step tasks, and building features autonomously with human oversight.

data.text: What Makes a Coding Agent Different

A coding agent is not just a chat assistant that writes code for you. It is an autonomous system that plans a series of actions, executes them, observes the results, and adapts. The agentic loop — Plan, Execute, Verify — is what distinguishes agents from traditional autocomplete or chat tools.

Every agentic coding workflow follows the same fundamental loop: the agent receives a goal, breaks it into steps, executes those steps by editing files or running commands, reads the results, and adjusts its plan. This loop repeats until the goal is achieved or the agent determines it needs human help.

data.caption: The agentic coding loop — plan, execute, verify, repeat
data.definition:
flowchart TD
  A[Receive Goal] --> B[Plan Steps]
  B --> C[Execute Changes]
  C --> D[Read Results / Run Tests]
  D --> E{Goal Met?}
  E -->|No| F[Adjust Plan]
  F --> C
  E -->|Yes| G[Complete]
  E -->|Stuck| H[Request Human Help]
  H --> G

data.text: The quality of the plan determines the quality of the final result. A good agent spends time understanding the codebase, identifying which files need changes, and ordering the steps to minimize conflicts. Rushed plans lead to messy diffs and broken code. The best prompt engineering for agents is actually prompt engineering for planning — the better the plan, the smoother the execution.

Agents execute plans using tools: read, write, and edit files; run terminal commands; execute tests; and query APIs. Each tool invocation is a discrete action that the agent chains together. The agent reads the output of each action to decide what to do next. This is why agentic coding requires robust error handling and observability — when something goes wrong at step 3, the agent needs to understand why before continuing.

After making changes, the agent runs tests, lint checks, and type checks to verify the changes work correctly. If a test fails, the agent reads the error, identifies what went wrong, and either retries with a different approach or adjusts the plan. This self-correcting behavior is what makes agents more powerful than single-shot code generation.

data.title: The human role shifts
data.text: With agents, your role shifts from writer to reviewer and director. You define the goal, review the plan, approve or redirect the approach, and do final code review on the output. You are the architect; the agent is the builder.

data.title: Best for:
items: Implementing a feature from a detailed specification
Migrating code from one framework or pattern to another
Writing tests for an existing module you did not write
Bulk updates across many similar files (renaming, upgrading, etc.)

data.title: Not ideal for:
items: Tasks requiring deep domain knowledge of your business logic
Security-critical code that requires human review at every step
Exploratory coding where you are still figuring out the approach

data.title: Be aware of these limitations:
items: Agents can make cascading errors — a wrong step early can compound
They may modify files you did not intend them to touch
Large plans can exceed the context window, requiring chunking
They cannot verify visual correctness (UI rendering, layout) without human review

data.title: Good agentic prompt
data.content: "I want to migrate our authentication from session-based to JWT. The current code uses express-session in middleware/auth.ts and server/routes.ts. The new implementation should use jsonwebtoken, store tokens in HttpOnly cookies, add a refresh token rotation, and maintain backward compatibility for 30 days. Follow the existing code style and patterns in the project. Do not modify the database schema."
data.code:
Good agentic prompt:

"I want to migrate our authentication from session-based to JWT. The current code uses `express-session` in `middleware/auth.ts` and `server/routes.ts`. The new implementation should use `jsonwebtoken`, store tokens in HttpOnly cookies, add a refresh token rotation, and maintain backward compatibility for 30 days. Follow the existing code style and patterns in the project. Do not modify the database schema."

data.title: Start small with agents
data.text: Do not start your first agentic coding session by asking for a complete feature. Start with a small, well-defined task like "refactor this single file to use async/await" and work your way up. Build trust in the agent's capabilities before giving it larger responsibilities.
